title: Proof-of-Hours for Medicaid Work Requirements
one_liner: A text-message-first evidence engine that helps gig, seasonal, cash and caregiving enrollees document the 80-hour requirement, paid by managed care plans and safety-net providers for each member retained.
customer: Medicaid managed care plans (revenue is capitation per member), FQHC networks, hospital systems and county health departments carrying uncompensated care. Not the states: federal law bars plans from determining compliance, but outreach and enrollee assistance are allowed.
problem: From 1 Jan 2027, expansion adults 19-64 must show 80 hours a month of work, study or service. CMS projects 2.3 million people lose coverage in FY2027, largely through paperwork failure rather than true non-compliance. Georgia Pathways enrolled only about 16,000 people against roughly 359,000 potentially eligible. Irregular earners (gig, day labor, home care, seasonal, informal) have no clean payroll record, and states mostly rely on payroll data that misses them.
solution: A multilingual SMS, WhatsApp and app 'hour ledger'. It pulls earnings from gig and payment platforms via consented bank or statement links, sends one-tap SMS attestations to employers and clients, and logs volunteer and caregiving hours via QR check-in at partner churches and food banks. It screens for exemptions (medical frailty, caregivers) and outputs the evidence pack in each state's format, with renewal reminders every six months. The member owns the data and the plan sees only consented status.
why_now: Nebraska began enforcement on 1 May 2026. CMS issued its interim final rule on 3 June 2026 defining verification and the 80-hour test, and states did outreach in mid-2026. The national start is 1 Jan 2027 with six-month renewals, and plans are amending contracts now.
revenue_model: A per-member retention bounty ($40-$120 per successful renewal) or PMPM of $2-$6 for high-risk members, paid by plans. FQHC and hospital subscriptions, and later state contracts for outreach.
non_obvious_insight: The fight is not over who is eligible but over who can prove it. Compliant-but-undocumented workers are a large share of those at risk. The party with the strongest incentive to close that gap is not the state but the plan or provider whose revenue disappears with each disenrolled member. Verified hours are a portable asset the member can reuse at every renewal.
first_30_days: Partner with one FQHC network in a live or early-start state such as Nebraska. Hand-run a pilot for 200 enrollees using SMS plus a form, and build evidence-pack templates that match the state portal. Pitch three regional plans on a no-upfront-cost, pay-per-member-retained deal. Get privacy and HIPAA review done before enrolling anyone.

title: IEP Chief of Staff for Special-Ed Parents
one_liner: Rich parents win school disputes with a paid educational advocate and paper trail; for $20/mo, give parents of the roughly 7.5M US students with IEPs a chief of staff who watches the legal clocks and logs every missed service minute.
customer: Parents of children with IEPs (autism, ADHD, dyslexia, speech and language delay), sold through state and local special-ed parent groups, parent training centers, pediatric practices, disability law clinics and credit unions.
problem: Districts arrive with a team; wealthy families bring an advocate ($150-400/hr) and an attorney. Federal enforcement was hollowed out (mass OSEP layoffs in October 2025, and reported moves of oversight to HHS and civil-rights enforcement to DOJ in June 2026), so parents are effectively on their own. Most violations are procedural (late evaluations, missing prior written notice, services not delivered) and go unnoticed because nobody keeps the clocks.
solution: Parent uploads the IEP and evaluations. The system builds the legal calendar (evaluation timelines from consent, meeting-notice windows, annual and triennial reviews, progress-report cadence), drafts records requests, creates a one-page pre-meeting brief (top asks plus data), and sends a same-day 'memorializing' follow-up email with prior-written-notice requests after meetings. It logs service minutes delivered vs promised, quantifying missed minutes for a compensatory-services claim, and scans the IEP for defects (no baselines, unmeasurable goals). Advocates are on-demand at $75 per 30 minutes, with a path to state complaint and due process.
why_now: The federal special-ed enforcement vacuum is documented and new as of late 2025 and mid-2026. IEP counts are rising, and LLMs can parse messy IEP PDFs and draft procedurally precise letters. Parent communities are organized on Facebook and Reddit and actively looking for help.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family; $75 advocate sessions with a revenue split to a vetted advocate co-op; $3-6 per member per month from parent centers, pediatric groups and credit unions; district-facing analytics sold only with parent consent, later.
non_obvious_insight: What the rich buy is not better argument but continuous procedural pressure: dated, written, specific requests. The subscription funds clock-watching and documentation, not advice. Parents who log service minutes turn 'I feel they're not delivering' into a quantified claim, and the paper trail is the evidence in any later dispute, so value compounds over time.
first_30_days: Publish a free IEP clock calculator and letter templates. Partner with admins of 10 state-level special-ed Facebook groups and concierge 30 families manually, measuring violations found. Convert those families to $20/mo and recruit 5 advocates for the on-demand tier.

title: Pay-on-Pass: Inspections Trigger Sub Payments
one_liner: Same-day payment to framers and foundation crews the moment the city inspection clears, financed against the builder's draw.
customer: Small private builders (20-300 homes a year) and their framing, foundation, plumbing and electrical subs, with a community lender or credit line as funding partner.
problem: Cities adopt AI plan review, filings surge (Honolulu applications +34% but permits issued +5%, backlog 9,252), and the bottleneck moves to post-permit inspections. Subs wait for the pass, then wait for payment: one in five subs waits 60+ days and GCs are 4x more likely than subs to be paid within 30 days. Crews are already vanishing, so slow payers lose them.
solution: A payment rail keyed to a third-party-verified milestone: inspection status pulled from municipal portals or a photo of the green tag. The sub is paid within 24 hours from a revolving credit facility, repaid from the builder's draw within 30 days. Builders also get a crew reliability ranking and inspection-queue analytics by jurisdiction and inspector, with photo pre-checks to raise first-time pass rates.
why_now: AI permitting is deploying now (Honolulu, Denver's $4.6M contract), shifting the constraint downstream. Immigration enforcement makes verified crews scarce, so pay speed has become a recruiting tool. Completions are down 27.1%.
revenue_model: 1.5-2.5% of released payments, paid by the builder for speed and crew retention, with an optional sub-paid instant-pay discount. Spread on credit line usage.
non_obvious_insight: The inspection pass is the only moment in construction that is third-party verified, timestamped and dispute-proof, which makes it the ideal payment trigger and collateral. Nobody uses it because the data sits in thousands of scattered municipal portals, but one builder in one metro needs only three or four.
first_30_days: Pick one metro and its three permit portals. Pilot with 3 builders and their 5 framing and foundation subs. Open a $100-200K line with a friendly community lender. Verify passes by hand and pay by ACH.

title: Licensed Cozy Games for Memory Care
one_liner: A turnkey activity program for senior living made of commercially licensed cozy indie games, in a kiosk kit that logs resident participation for compliance paperwork.
customer: Activity directors and operators of memory care, assisted living and skilled nursing communities, starting with independents and small regional chains of 5-50 sites. They pay about $199-349 a month per community plus a $349-499 kit.
problem: Nursing homes must run person-centered activity programs and document participation (CMS F-tag 679). Directors are short on budget and staff time. Existing tech is expensive proprietary hardware such as projector tables or VR. Consumer games are the wrong fit: their licences forbid commercial and public use, and they have reading-heavy UI, timers and fail states.
solution: A curated library of 30-50 indie titles that are gentle by design: no fail states, no timers, big targets, little text, familiar themes like gardening, cooking and tidying. Developers grant commercial, DRM-free licences for a revenue share. Each title runs in a locked kiosk launcher on a docked handheld or mini-PC to the TV, with big-button controllers. Staff get 5-minute group-play cards and a one-tap participation log that exports to activity documentation. It is positioned as activity programming, not therapy, so it makes no clinical claims.
why_now: About 4M Americans turn 65 each year through 2027, so demand for senior activities is rising. Handheld PCs are cheap and reliable. Senior living operators are already piloting games (for example the Belmont Village pilot of a cognitive game). Steam's glut of cozy games means many strong titles with dormant back-catalogs that earn nothing.
revenue_model: Monthly subscription per community, a hardware kit margin, and 40-50% of subscription revenue paid to developers by playtime. Later: enterprise contracts with chains, and reimbursement or wellness-budget channels.
non_obvious_insight: Steam keys are personal-use licences. Only the developer can grant commercial or public-performance rights, and a dormant catalog makes them say yes for a small guarantee. The traits that make cozy games sell are exactly what dementia-friendly design needs. And directors buy relief from documentation and set-up time, not cognitive outcomes. VCs file this under 'brain-training edtech', while an insider sees a licensing arbitrage plus a compliance workflow.
first_30_days: License 8-10 cozy titles, offering $500 minimum guarantees plus revenue share. Assemble 5 kits at about $400 each. Offer free 4-week pilots to 5 local communities through activity-director Facebook groups and state activity-professional associations. Log participation minutes per resident. Convert pilots to paid at week 5.

title: SNAP Rules Engine for Independent Grocers
one_liner: An API and POS plug-in that classifies every UPC against each state's changing SNAP soda and candy rules.
customer: Independent grocers and convenience stores in states with SNAP restrictions, and the POS and EBT vendors that serve them.
problem: 22 states have SNAP soda and candy restrictions in effect or pending, definitions differ by state, and a June 2026 ruling (Aragon v. Rollins) blocked waivers in five states, so rules keep flipping.
solution: A maintained UPC-level eligibility database by state and effective date, delivered as a POS plug-in and API with audit logs for SNAP authorization defense.
why_now: Patchwork state waivers and court reversals in 2026 mean retailers carry compliance liability without product-level data.
revenue_model: $30-60 per store per month, plus license fees from POS vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Court-driven rule flips make this a recurring data subscription rather than a one-time setup, and the liability sits with retailers who have no tooling.
first_30_days: Classify the top 5,000 UPCs for four states, pilot in 20 independent stores and one POS vendor, and set up a rule-change alert feed.

title: Year-Round Books for Immigrant-Community Tax Storefronts
one_liner: Give community tax preparers WhatsApp-native, in-language AI bookkeeping so they can serve their small-business clients all year.
customer: Independent tax storefronts in Latino, Vietnamese, Korean, Chinese and other immigrant communities, each serving 100-500 micro-business clients (taquerias, nail salons, owner-operator truckers, cleaners, roofing crews) who show up with a shoebox once a year.
problem: The clients have no monthly books. Preparers can't do year-round bookkeeping without adding headcount, and they cannot afford Intuit's or H&R Block's offering. Silicon Valley assumes better AI will close the trust gap, but these owners trust a person who speaks their language.
solution: White-label intake through WhatsApp, WeChat or KakaoTalk: the client sends receipt photos and voice notes in their language, and AI drafts the ledger and a monthly P&L. The preparer reviews exceptions in a queue and sends a plain-language summary. Sales tax, payroll deposits and quarterly estimated tax reminders are included. All output carries the preparer's brand.
why_now: Multilingual and code-switched voice transcription became reliable in 2025-26. IRS Direct File ended for 2026, and Intuit cut 17% of staff while opening about 600 offices and 20 TurboTax storefronts, which suggests trust stays human and local.
revenue_model: $99/month per storefront plus $12 per client per month, or a 30% revenue share on a $150 per client monthly bookkeeping fee.
non_obvious_insight: The trust problem is already solved by a human who is embedded in the community. What the preparer lacks is leverage, and the incumbents are hiring storefronts, not selling to them. AI turns a seasonal tax business into a year-round one.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 storefronts in one metro through ITIN and tax-prep associations and Spanish-language radio. Pilot with five clients each on WhatsApp Business. Charge nothing until the storefronts see retention and added revenue, then set the per-client price.

title: Clickwrap Gatekeeper: Agents Buy Contract Counsel
one_liner: An API agents call before clicking 'I agree'. It returns clause-level risk against the principal's delegated-authority policy, plus a signed archive of exactly what was accepted.
customer: Wallet-holding consumer and enterprise agents, and the platforms that run them, paying $0.02-$0.50 per document evaluation plus an evidence-archive fee per acceptance. Agent-wallet and browser-agent vendors are the natural embedders.
problem: Agents will accept tens of thousands of ToS, DPAs, auto-renewals, arbitration waivers and data-resale clauses for people and companies. Courts increasingly treat automated assent as binding, so the open legal question is the scope of the agent's authority. Agents can read a contract, but none has a legal-grade policy engine or a defensible evidence trail. Amazon's fight with Perplexity over agent access is one visible example of that unsettled authority.
solution: check(url_or_text, policy) diffs the document, hash-cached and versioned, against the principal's policy: max liability, no auto-renew beyond 30 days, no mandatory arbitration, no resale of personal data. It returns ALLOW, ESCALATE or REFUSE with cited clauses. On ALLOW it snapshots the page (hash, timestamp, screenshot) into a tamper-evident log so the principal can later prove what was accepted. A diff feed alerts the principal when terms change on services already accepted. It is positioned as a policy engine, not legal advice, with law-firm-authored policy packs.
why_now: Agent authority is the live legal question of 2026, with law-firm memos on 'authority to bind' and litigation over agent access. Payment protocols such as AP2 mandates and ACP mean agents now click through payment terms without a human present. Browser agents are in production use.
revenue_model: Metered evaluation (first-seen documents priced high, cache hits nearly free), an evidence-archive fee per accepted contract, enterprise policy packs, and a marketplace for lawyer-written policy templates with a revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of legal risk in the agent economy is not the model's hallucination but the tiny irrevocable assent. Because most ToS are near-identical templates, one shared cache amortizes legal analysis across millions of agents, which no single company can do for itself. Lawyers become policy authors rather than reviewers, and gross margin exceeds 90% once the cache is warm.
first_30_days: Crawl and index ToS, privacy and DPA pages for the top 5,000 SaaS and e-commerce sites and cluster them into templates. Publish a free MCP server with 1,000 free checks. Recruit 3 advisory lawyers to seed policy templates. Pitch agent-wallet startups and browser-agent vendors to embed it as a pre-payment check, and start charging in month 2.

title: TAKE IT DOWN Desk for Small Platforms
one_liner: Outsourced 48-hour notice-and-removal operations (intake, requester verification, adjudication, audit logs) for forums, hosts and indie social apps.
customer: Small and mid-size platforms with user-generated content (forums, image hosts, creator platforms, community apps, dating apps) that have no trust-and-safety staff, plus web hosts and their counsel.
problem: The FTC began enforcing the TAKE IT DOWN Act on 19 May 2026, wrote to 15 large platforms including Discord, Reddit and Automattic, and lists civil penalties of $53,088 per violation. Coverage reaches forums with user content. The 48-hour clock is real, but the request process is abusable, since false takedown notices can be weaponised, and platforms must verify that the requester is the depicted person without collecting more sensitive imagery.
solution: A hosted intake endpoint and a staffed desk. It offers identity-light requester verification (hash matching in the style of StopNCII), adjudication by trained reviewers with escalation, removal of known identical copies across the customer's site, an appeal and counter-notice path, and FTC-ready audit logs. Follow-the-sun contractors with wellness support provide coverage. Requires legal review per jurisdiction.
why_now: Enforcement started in May 2026, the FTC opened a complaint portal (TakeItDown.ftc.gov), and nonconsensual deepfake volume is rising. Small platforms cannot afford in-house teams, and the statute imposes a duty to act with no penalty for false requests.
revenue_model: $500-5k per month base plus $15-40 per resolved case, with enterprise SLAs.
non_obvious_insight: The statute mandates speed but not accuracy, so the operational risk is over-removal and abuse. The product is adjudication with a paper trail, not filtering, and the buyer's fear is an FTC letter, not a bad user.
first_30_days: Sell through forum-software hosting partners, web-hosting providers and indie creator platforms. Train a contractor pool in handling sensitive imagery and stand up intake for 10 pilot communities.

title: Reverse Mzigo: Parents' Farm Feeds Nairobi Kids
one_liner: A weekly, consolidated truck route that moves food from rural parents' farms to their own adult children in Nairobi estates, paid by the children, turning an informal favour into a subscription that gives parents a dignified monthly income.
customer: Urban salaried Kenyans (25-45) who already receive 'mzigo' (parcels of maize flour, arrowroot, sweet potatoes, bananas, sukuma, eggs, kienyeji chicken) from their rural mothers. Suppliers are the mothers and other smallholders in their village cluster. Friends and neighbours of the children are the natural second wave of buyers.
problem: Farm-to-consumer startups keep dying on trust and customer acquisition: urban buyers do not trust unknown farmers and farmers do not trust unknown buyers. Yet a huge informal flow already exists in the opposite direction from the usual assumption: parents send food to their city children by matatu drivers and bus parcel counters, unreliably, unweighed, unrecorded, with spoilage and no payment trail. The children also quietly want to support their parents but handouts hurt parental pride and get 'shared' with relatives.
solution: Village-cluster pickup and Nairobi last-mile drops, organised by a WhatsApp group per village and a simple order cycle. The child orders or subscribes (say KES 2,000-4,000 per fortnight) and pays by M-Pesa. The parent gets paid the same day on delivery of graded, weighed produce at the village collection point. The platform handles packaging, a consolidated Saturday truck or van, cold-ish handling for chicken and eggs, and a photo receipt with 'from Mama Wanjiku' provenance. Buying food from mum becomes a socially acceptable remittance that preserves her dignity and creates predictable monthly income. Over time it adds friends-of-the-family boxes, bulk orders for church and workplace groups, and inputs credit for the mothers repaid out of box sales.
why_now: Urban food inflation and food-safety anxiety have pushed Nairobi professionals to look for known-source food. Mobile-money receipts and WhatsApp Business make the order-to-payment loop nearly free to run. Delivery infrastructure (van pooling, boda last-mile) is cheap enough in Nairobi estates to support a weekly consolidated route. Most Nairobi residents keep strong up-country ties, so the founder's own network is a zero-cost acquisition channel.
revenue_model: Delivery and platform margin of about 12-18% on box value (parents keep roughly 60-70%, transport and packaging the rest), plus a small subscription or priority-delivery fee. Later, inputs and micro-loan referrals to the mothers, and corporate or church bulk orders.
non_obvious_insight: The customer for rural produce is the farmer's own child, not a stranger. Family trust is a free, pre-built distribution network, and it removes the customer acquisition and trust costs that kill farm-to-fork startups. It also means the product is really a disguised remittance channel: paying for goods is a more comfortable way to support parents than sending cash.
first_30_days: Use your own parents' village and 10 neighbouring mothers, plus 40 Nairobi households from your WhatsApp contacts (school, church, workplace groups). Run one Saturday route on a hired pickup with a Google Form for orders and M-Pesa till for payment. Measure spoilage, on-time rate and how often children reorder, then add a second village once the unit economics on the first route are positive.

title: Independent Audits for Per-Outcome Agent Invoices
one_liner: The DoubleVerify of AI agents: sample and verify the resolutions, meetings and approvals you were billed for, then claim credits for the fakes.
customer: Finance, procurement and support-ops leaders at companies paying $50k-$5M a year to outcome-priced agent vendors (support resolutions, AP processing, claims, scheduling).
problem: Vendors have moved from seats to outcomes. Reportedly, Zendesk narrowed billing to LLM-verified 'resolutions' at about $1.20-$1.50 each and HubSpot's customer agent charges about $0.50 per resolved conversation. The vendor defines and grades its own outcome, and buyers cannot tell a real resolution from a customer who gave up. Step two of falling token prices is vendors with an incentive to over-count outcomes.
solution: A read-only connector to the buyer's helpdesk, CRM or ERP that re-derives outcomes independently from reopen rates, repeat contacts in 7-14 days, silent abandonment, escalation to humans and sentiment. Sample about 300 outcomes a month for blind human plus LLM review. Deliver a monthly invoice integrity report with the false-outcome rate and a credit-claim packet aligned to the contract's dispute window.
why_now: Outcome pricing became mainstream in 2026, and Deloitte published guidance in June 2026 on accounting for it, which signals CFO attention. Buyers paying per outcome have no independent measurement.
revenue_model: 10-20% of credits recovered plus a $2-6k/month subscription. The buy side pays first to avoid conflict, and vendors may later pay for an audited badge.
non_obvious_insight: Ad tech showed that when sellers measure their own outcomes, a third-party verifier becomes a category (DoubleVerify, IAS). Agent outcome pricing recreates that conflict with almost no independent measurement, and the earliest data is anonymous benchmarks of false-resolution rates.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 companies using Fin, Zendesk or HubSpot agents through support-ops communities. Run a free or contingency retrospective audit of 3 months of invoices and publish anonymized false-resolution rates to seed demand.

title: Exposure Response Desk for Vibe-Coded Apps
one_liner: A fix-and-legal-decision service for founders whose AI-built apps leaked user data, delivering an RLS lockdown, an access-log check and a breach-notification memo.
customer: Non-technical founders and small businesses that shipped apps on Lovable, Bolt, Replit or Cursor with a Supabase backend, and small agencies that build such apps for local clients. They pay $149-$499 per incident plus $29/month monitoring.
problem: On Sept 25, 2026 UpGuard reported about 16,000 Supabase databases publicly exposing names, home addresses, phone numbers, passwords, auth tokens, private conversations and license plate records. AI coding tools write SQL migrations where Row-Level Security defaults to off, and founders never turn it on. An earlier flaw, CVE-2025-48757, exposed 170+ Lovable apps. Owners do not know how to fix it without breaking the app, whether anyone actually accessed the data, or whether they now have a legal duty to notify users and regulators.
solution: Not another scanner, since ShipSafe and VibeAppScanner already exist. This is a response desk. (1) The owner authorizes a read-only check on their own project. (2) The tool generates and tests an RLS policy pull request for common patterns (owner-only rows, public read and owner write, storage buckets) that does not break the app. (3) It reviews available Supabase API and Postgres logs to estimate whether anonymous-key access from unknown sources occurred. (4) A partner privacy attorney's state-by-state and GDPR decision tree produces a notification-or-not memo. (5) It drafts user notices and an evidence packet for the owner's cyber insurer. Continuous monitoring is upsell.
why_now: The UpGuard disclosure is three days old, and Cursor AI is the fastest-growing Glimpse trend of 2026 (+2,213%), with Cyber Insurance up 763% on Exploding Topics. Mass disclosures of this kind will keep recurring as more founders ship AI-built apps. Legal clocks (GDPR 72 hours, state laws with 30-60 day windows) create urgency at exactly the moment the owner learns of the exposure.
revenue_model: $149 lockdown-only tier, $499 lockdown plus log review plus notification memo and letters, $29/month continuous monitoring, and $99/client wholesale packages for agencies. Later: referral fees from cyber insurers and privacy counsel.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone sells detection. Nobody sells the 'now what', and the mission-critical question for an owner is legal, not technical. The trigger is public and fresh: UpGuard found ~16,000 exposed Supabase databases, the root cause is that AI-written migrations leave RLS off, and Supabase's CISO says security 'ultimately remains a shared responsibility' (https://startupfortune.com/upguard-found-16000-supabase-databases-leaking-user-data-to-the-open-web/). CVE-2025-48757 previously exposed 170+ Lovable apps, and the common failure is founders who cannot debug RLS (https://www.superblocks.com/blog/lovable-vulnerabilities). The scanner market already exists (https://vibeappscanner.com/lovable-security), which means paid demand is proven while the response step remains unowned. Cursor AI's +2,213% growth is the #1 item at https://meetglimpse.com/trends/.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build the read-only exposure checker that owners run on their own project, plus an RLS policy generator for the five most common patterns. Days 8-15: co-author a 'Supabase RLS was off, what now? (24-hour plan)' guide with a privacy attorney and publish it for SEO and Reddit (r/lovable, r/supabase, Indie Hackers). Days 16-30: sell 20 lockdown fixes at $149-$199 and sign 2 small agencies at wholesale rates. Skip scanning anyone's databases without their authorization.

title: Payroll and Proof-of-Trust for Household Staff
one_liner: A WhatsApp payroll, advance and verified-record product for Nigeria's drivers, housekeepers, nannies and gatemen, paid for by their employers.
customer: Middle- and upper-income households in Lagos and Abuja (Lekki, Ikoyi, VI, Ikeja GRA, Maitama) that employ domestic staff. Placement agencies as a channel. Diaspora children who pay for home-care of ageing parents.
problem: Millions of household workers are paid in cash or ad-hoc transfers, with no records, no pension, no health cover and no credit history. Employers act as lender of last resort, giving 3-5 untracked advances a year for school fees and emergencies. That breeds resentment, sudden resignations and theft accusations. Placement agencies charge roughly a month's salary and rely on 'guarantor forms' that everyone knows can be faked. Staff are excluded from credit even after 10 years of steady pay.
solution: The employer sets each worker's salary and pay date on WhatsApp and pays through the platform. The system runs an NIN/BVN check at hire, records every advance and auto-deducts repayment from next month's pay, and keeps a payslip history. The worker gets a wallet, an optional micro-pension contribution and health-cover add-on, and a payment-history record that lenders can use for the first genuine loan of their life. Agencies get a 'verified staff' badge and a share of revenue in return for onboarding their clients.
why_now: Wallet and bank-account penetration among lower-income workers is now high enough that most domestic staff already hold OPay, Moniepoint or PalmPay accounts. NIN/BVN verification APIs are cheap. Salary advances and lending are moving into the regulated FCCPC and CBN perimeter, and households are more cost-squeezed and more digital than in 2020. Voice-note and WhatsApp interfaces in English, Pidgin and Yoruba are finally reliable.
revenue_model: Employer subscription of about N2,000-3,000 per worker per month. A small fee on advances routed through employer-funded 'advance limits'. Commissions on micro-pension, health-cover and eventual worker microloans. Placement-agency referral share and verified-staff certificate fees.
non_obvious_insight: The real customer is the employer's peace of mind, not the worker's financial inclusion. Households will pay to stop the awkward informal-lender relationship and the fear of being scammed by staff with fake guarantors. The worker's payment history is a credit dataset that no bureau holds, and the employer pays to create it.
first_30_days: Ship a WhatsApp bot with a simple payslip and advance ledger, using a bank-partner payout API. Sign 8-10 placement agencies in Lekki, Ikoyi and Maitama and pilot with 100 households through their client lists and estate WhatsApp groups. Charge from day one, since these households are not price-sensitive. Use the first 300 workers' history to design a pilot micro-loan with a partner MFB.

title: Borrowing-Base Verification for Recycler Lenders
one_liner: A drone-and-assay 'borrowing base as a service' that lets specialty lenders finance recyclers against verified inventory.
customer: Asset-based lenders, factoring firms and specialty commodity funds (primary payers), plus recyclers who need working capital against bales, black mass, swarf and scrap.
problem: After Ascend's Chapter 11, Li-Cycle's bankruptcy and the PET reclaimer closures, credit for recyclers is tight. Lenders cannot verify what is in the pile: volume, grade, moisture, title and price risk. Commodity-finance frauds, shrink and theft are a real concern.
solution: Monthly drone and LiDAR volumetrics, density and grade sampling, scale-house data integration, title and lien checks, and index-based mark-to-market. Lender-ready certificates with shrink alerts.
why_now: The 2025-26 recycling failures made lenders cautious, while BIS-driven domestic feed flows and price volatility make inventory more valuable and more mispriced.
revenue_model: $1.5-4K per site per month, plus basis points on facilities placed.
non_obvious_insight: Recyclers are not short of collateral; lenders are short of trust in it. Collateral management firms serve large metal traders and skip the $5-50M recyclers.
first_30_days: Talk to 10 ABL lenders and 2 factoring firms. Pilot with 3 recyclers refinancing now. Build a volumetrics pipeline on off-the-shelf drones and photogrammetry.

title: Allergen Drift Alerts for School Cafeterias
one_liner: A weekly diff engine over the open Open Food Facts and USDA Branded Food Products data that tells school nutrition directors when a product on their order guide silently changed its allergens.
customer: K-12 school district food service directors and their purchasing co-ops and state agencies (about 13,000 US districts). A parent-facing paid alert tier for families of children with severe allergies is a secondary market.
problem: Distributors substitute products and manufacturers reformulate without notice. After sesame became the ninth major US allergen, some bakeries began adding sesame on purpose. Directors keep allergen lists in spreadsheets built from last year's spec sheets. Recalls are announced only after exposure, and cooks get blamed for what is really supplier drift.
solution: Ingest the district's order guide (Sysco, US Foods, Gordon Food Service item lists) and match SKUs to GTINs. Track ingredient statements and allergen declarations over time using Open Food Facts revision history and the monthly USDA Branded Food Products (GDSN) releases. Send a weekly 'allergen drift' report and immediate alerts when an allergen is added, a 'may contain' changes, or a substitution appears. Auto-update the district's allergen matrix and menu labels.
why_now: Branded-food data goes stale quickly and USDA now publishes monthly GDSN updates. Reformulation churn following the 2023 sesame rule and supply-chain substitutions is high. Open Food Facts has reached scale, and diffing it is cheap while no one sells the diff.
revenue_model: USD 500-1,500 per district per year, tiered by SKU count. State-agency or co-op bulk licenses. Parent alert tier at USD 3-5 per month.
non_obvious_insight: Most cafeteria allergen incidents trace to a silent supplier change, not to cooking error, so the value is monitoring the upstream data exhaust that already exists and is free. Directors will pay for peace of mind and liability evidence, not for a new database.
first_30_days: Build the diff pipeline for the 300 most common K-12 SKUs. Publish a free weekly 'Allergen Drift Report' newsletter aimed at food service directors and state school nutrition associations to build trust. Offer 5 districts a free SKU-matching of their full order guide. Convert to paid alerts with the first two districts that catch a real change.

title: Show Safe: Compliance and Theft Registry
one_liner: An operating layer for card-show and fan-convention promoters that handles vendor tax permits, insurance certificates, secure check-in and a shared stolen-slab registry.
customer: Promoters of card shows, comic and anime cons (thousands across the US) and vendor associations.
problem: State rules put promoters on the hook for collecting tax on admissions and verifying vendor permits (RI, NY and TX guidance). Armed robberies and thefts of collectors and vendors spiked in 2026 (CNN, April 2026; $100k stolen from a Burbank card store; about $10k stolen at Anime NYC). Promoters run on spreadsheets and Facebook groups.
solution: Vendor onboarding with per-state permit and tax-ID verification and insurance certificate upload, table booking and payments, badge check-in and out logs, incident reporting, and a registry of stolen graded-card cert numbers and serials that vendors and stores can scan-check. Optional admissions-tax filing.
why_now: The 2026 theft wave and insurer scrutiny make promoters want safety and paperwork rigor. The registry's value grows with every show that joins.
revenue_model: $150-500 per show SaaS, ~1.5% on payments, registry API access for stores, and insurance referrals.
non_obvious_insight: Promoters are the choke point where thousands of vendors meet, so the stolen-goods network effect belongs to whoever sees vendor flow. Compliance is the reason to sign up, and the registry is the moat.
first_30_days: Sign 10 local promoters with a free first show. Seed the registry from public theft reports on social media. Charge from show two.

title: Side-Selling Early Warning for Milk and Coffee Coops
one_liner: A churn-prediction and targeted-advance service that tells dairy and coffee cooperatives which farmers are about to side-sell to cash brokers, and triggers the right cash intervention before the volume walks away.
customer: Managers and boards of medium-sized dairy cooperatives (about 2,000-10,000 farmers), coffee cooperative societies and factories, and mid-sized processors that buy from farmer groups. They pay because lost throughput hits fixed factory costs and credit recovery.
problem: Side-selling is the silent killer of Kenyan coops. Farmers sell milk to hawkers and raw-milk traders, or coffee cherry to cash buyers, who pay on the spot, while the coop pays monthly or later and then deducts for feeds, inputs, AI services and loans. Deliveries fade slowly, not suddenly, so managers notice too late. Side-selling spikes when a farmer's net pay is squeezed by deductions, when payment is late, or in cash-crunch weeks such as January and other school fee dates, funerals and sickness. Coops respond with lectures and warnings instead of predicting and fixing the cash gap.
solution: Ingest the coop's delivery and payment history (usually already exported from the weighing or dairy management software). A simple gradient-boosted or rule-based model scores each farmer weekly for side-selling risk using delivery drift, missed pay days, deductions as a share of gross, days since last payment, seasonality and school-term calendars. The coop gets a daily short list for its field officer, with SMS or voice-call scripts in the local language. The intervention is a coop-funded, capped advance or deduction holiday for at-risk farmers in their predicted cash-crunch window, since the coop already holds the delivered stock and the farmer's record as collateral. It measures recovered litres or kilos against a control group.
why_now: Global arabica prices spiked to record highs in 2025 and pulled cherry towards cash brokers in Kenya, at the same time as coffee-sector reforms push coops to pay faster and more transparently. Weighing scales and dairy management software have digitised delivery data at many coops over the last five years, so the data now exists. M-Pesa bulk disbursement makes weekly or on-demand advances cheap. Modern ML tooling makes a credible model a two-week job rather than a research project. I could not verify current legal specifics, so confirm the latest coffee and dairy regulations and data-protection obligations (coop as data controller) before pilots.
revenue_model: Performance fee of roughly 5-10% of recovered volume value (paid from the additional milk or cherry that stays in the coop), or a SaaS retainer of a few tens of thousands of shillings per month per coop. Later, licensing the model to processors and lenders who want a farmer reliability signal.
non_obvious_insight: Side-selling is not disloyalty, it is a rational response to cash-flow timing. The winning intervention is not a scolding letter but a small advance placed at the right moment, funded by the coop's own working capital. It is also predictable from delivery patterns weeks before it happens, because farmers taper deliveries before they stop. Most agritech sells farmers new products, whereas here the buyer is the institution that quietly loses 10% or more of its volume.
first_30_days: Get 24 months of delivery and payment CSVs from one or two coops, ideally through your own parents' society or the manager you know personally. Build the risk model in a notebook, deliver a top-200 at-risk list plus a script, and run a 60-day test where half the list gets the SMS and advance offer and half does not. Agree to be paid only on retained volume compared to the control group, and use the result as the case study for the next five coops.

title: Passive Elder Wellness Checks From Water Flow
one_liner: A daily 'your parent used water normally' text built from a clip-on flow sensor or a utility's smart-meter feed, sold to adult children as flood protection first and wellness second.
customer: Adult-child caregivers of solo-living 75+ parents and early-dementia patients (about $14/month), resold through home-care agencies and Area Agencies on Aging. Secondary buyers are water utilities with interval (AMI) meters that want a customer-care program.
problem: Wearables get abandoned, cameras get refused, and 69% of adults 50+ are uncomfortable sharing health data with AI tools. Yet 27% of Americans 65+ live alone, 59M family caregivers work unpaid, and agencies lose 77-80% of caregivers a year. China's 'Are You Dead?' check-in app topping paid charts in Jan 2026 shows families will pay for the thinnest possible 'are they OK' signal.
solution: A clip-on flow sensor on the main line, or opt-in utility interval data, plus fixture-signature disaggregation, learns each home's routine (first morning tap, flushes, showers, kitchen). It alerts on no morning use by a set hour, repeated 3 a.m. flushes (wandering), a tap left running, a sudden drop in showers (an early hygiene and dementia marker) and scald-level hot water. An optional auto-shutoff valve stops floods. The family gets a daily 'all normal' text, with an escalation tree to family, then the agency, then a welfare check.
why_now: Drought pressure has pushed utilities to roll out interval meters and customer portals for leak detection, so the data already exists. Medicaid cuts (about $911B) and shrinking Medicare Advantage benefits push more seniors onto unpaid family care. Older-adult tech acceptance is rising (23% of 65+ now use ChatGPT, up from 10%). The 2026 China check-in app proved mass demand for minimalist check-ins.
revenue_model: $14/month per home plus a $79 kit. Agencies pay $6 per client per month for white-label. Utilities pay a license or revenue share of roughly $0.25-0.50 per enrolled account per month once AMI opt-in works.
non_obvious_insight: Water is the one utility no person can skip, fake or forget to charge, and no eldercare company sells it. It sidesteps the privacy and compliance objections that kill cameras and wearables. The 'leak and flood protection' pitch lets a proud parent accept something they would refuse as 'monitoring'. Japan's kettle-based 'mimamori' watch-over services showed appliance-use check-ins work, and water is the version that scales on utility infrastructure.
first_30_days: Buy 100 off-the-shelf clip-on flow monitors. Pitch three local home-care agencies and two caregiver Facebook groups a '$99 parent flood-and-check-in kit', and ship 50. Build the routine-anomaly model on consented data over 60-90 days. Then offer one small AMI-equipped utility an opt-in pilot using interval data.

title: Hours Wallet for Medicaid Work Requirements
one_liner: A text-first tool that proves 80 hours or $580 a month of work for gig and cash earners, paid by Medicaid plans and clinics that lose money when members drop off.
customer: Payers: Medicaid managed-care plans, FQHCs and hospital financial-counseling teams paying per enrolled or retained member. Users: adults 19-64 in the Medicaid expansion group with irregular income (gig, seasonal, cash, self-employed).
problem: The CMS interim final rule (June 1, 2026) requires about 43 states plus DC to enforce 80 hours per month of work, service or school, or at least $580 per month of earnings, by January 1, 2027, at application and renewal. If compliance cannot be verified the person gets only 30 calendar days to prove it. Proof means pay stubs and letters from employers or volunteer organizations. Arkansas's 2018 requirement cost 18,000 people coverage for failing to meet work or reporting rules.
solution: SMS or WhatsApp-first app that (a) connects gig-platform exports or bank deposits to test the $580 income alternative, (b) sends one-tap timestamped attestation links to a boss, food-bank coordinator or volunteer supervisor, (c) auto-formats the state's monthly report and files it, (d) alerts the member before the 30-day cure window closes, and (e) screens for exemptions such as parents or caretakers of children under 14 and disability. It gives the payer a dashboard of at-risk members.
why_now: The federal rule is final as of June 2026 and states must be live by January 1, 2027 (some earlier, with Nebraska reportedly starting May 1, 2026). Self-attestation is only allowed for 2027, after which documentation is required, so 2027 is the last cheap window to build a member base and data habit before documentation hardens.
revenue_model: Per-member-per-month or success fee per retained member from MCOs and FQHCs (about $3-$10/member/month or a bounty per successful renewal), with a free tier for members; secondary revenue from employer-attestation seats for staffing and home-care agencies.
non_obvious_insight: States must first use payroll and other data to verify compliance, which leaves the residual, hardest population (cash, gig and self-employed workers) exactly where a proof tool is needed. Payers, not members, have the money, because each lost member is lost capitation revenue. The CMS rule text (https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/medicaid-community-engagement-requirement-certain-individuals-interim-final-rule-comment-period-cms) gives the $580 alternative, 30-day cure period and exemptions, and KFF's data brief cites the 18,000 Arkansas coverage losses (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/issue-brief/understanding-the-intersection-of-medicaid-and-work-what-does-the-data-say/). Reddit was unreachable, so the r/personalfinance and r/legaladvice 'how do I prove my hours?' demand is forecast from the rule and explainers rather than quoted threads.
first_30_days: Build the $580 income test and attestation-link flow for Nebraska (reportedly already live) plus one January 2027 state. Approach 2 FQHCs and one regional MCO or hospital financial counseling team for a free pilot, and give the tool free to food banks and legal-aid groups as distribution. Aim for 200 pilot members, then convert the clinics to a per-member fee with retained-coverage data as the proof.

title: Worker-Owned Agentic Back-Office Cooperatives
one_liner: A franchise-in-a-box that helps laid-off finance and admin staff form co-ops running agent-leveraged bookkeeping, payroll and billing services for local small businesses, keeping the surplus themselves.
customer: Small businesses (5-50 employees) pay $600-2,500 a month. The co-ops pay a 5-8% platform fee, and are financed by cooperative-lending CDFIs, SBA microloans and workforce boards.
problem: The AI productivity dividend flows to platform owners while back-office workers lose jobs. Small businesses lack trusted human accountability (Bench's Dec 2024 shutdown stranded about 35k SMBs), and pure-AI bookkeepers still need a human on the hook.
solution: Co-op charter templates under state worker-co-op law, a shared agent stack (ledger automation, document intake, reconciliation) so each member handles 30-60 clients, a shared E&O policy, bank account and brand, client acquisition through local CPAs and chambers, and patronage dividends. Six-week onboarding.
why_now: Agentic accounting can now handle high-volume categorisation and reconciliation, finance-ops layoffs are rising, Bench's collapse left an opening, and co-op-friendly state laws and CDFI capital exist.
revenue_model: 5-8% of co-op revenue as a platform fee, tooling margin and $5-10k implementation fees per co-op.
non_obvious_insight: Ownership is the lever: workers who own the margin adopt agents fully, whereas employees hide productivity gains for fear of layoff. The scarce asset is trusted local human accountability, and agents supply the cost side.
first_30_days: Find 8-10 laid-off bookkeepers and controllers in one metro through layoff communities. Form a pilot co-op with a co-op legal clinic. Sign 15 SMB clients via three local CPAs and a chamber and run the first monthly closes.

title: End-of-Life Pet Cell Banking via Aftercare Providers
one_liner: Sell a living-cell keepsake through pet crematories and euthanasia vets, and build a consented canine and feline cell-and-genome atlas for research.
customer: Grieving pet owners pay $249-399 per animal. Pet crematories, in-home euthanasia vets and cemeteries are distribution partners. Vet-pharma, AI-drug-discovery and academic groups license the consented, de-identified cell lines and genomes.
problem: Owners will pay for memorials, but the only 'living' option today is boutique cloning-linked gene banking at roughly $1,600+ that almost nobody hears about at the moment they need it. Aftercare providers touch millions of pets a year and have no biotech product. At the same time, AI-driven and vet drug discovery lack breed-annotated cell lines and genomes tied to full medical histories, and proprietary biological datasets are commanding large valuations (Basecamp raised $140M; Tempus is assembling 100k genomes).
solution: A low-cost collection kit (skin punch biopsy in transport medium, chilled shipping) handled by a vet or trained aftercare staff within 24-48 hours of death. A contract lab establishes and cryopreserves fibroblast lines for 20+ years, and optional whole-genome sequencing is included. Owners choose 'keep only' or a discounted 'keep and donate to research'. Consented lines plus medical-record metadata go into a research atlas that partners license.
why_now: High-profile celebrity pet cloning in late 2025 made living pet genetics a mainstream conversation. Whole-genome sequencing now costs roughly $100-200, and proprietary datasets are what AI-bio investors pay for. Pet aftercare is a large, emotionally trusted channel that no biotech has approached, and vet-shortage-driven consolidation is pushing clinics toward add-on revenue.
revenue_model: $249-399 per animal plus $60 per year storage. Partners earn $40-60 per kit. Research licensing of consented lines and genomes at $500-2,000 per line with metadata, plus dataset subscriptions. Unit costs are about $120-180 for culture and cryostorage.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource for pet biotech is not technology but trusted access to animals at the moment of death, and that access sits with crematories and euthanasia vets, not labs. Framing the purchase as optionality (cloning, future cell therapy) plus a donation option turns a grief moment into a data flywheel.
first_30_days: Contract an academic or commercial cell-banking lab for a validated tissue-to-line protocol. Sign 3-5 pet crematories or in-home euthanasia practices in one metro, and place 20 kits at a $99 introductory price. Recruit a supervising veterinarian and create an owner consent form covering research use. Take the first 30-50 lines to two vet-pharma or AI-biotech prospects for a data pilot.

title: Claims Desk for Government-Paid Childcare
one_liner: A medical-billing-style revenue-cycle service that turns small providers' attendance sheets into clean subsidy and universal-program claims and advances the cash within 48 hours.
customer: Family child care homes and one-to-three-site centers in states and cities with subsidy or universal-care programs, such as NYC and New Mexico (the latter from memory).
problem: As governments become the payer (universal-care promises, 2026 tax credits, tighter CCDF rules), providers face attendance logs, eligibility recertification, claim rejections, 30-60 day payment delays and fraud audits. Margins are thin, payroll is about 70% of cost, and the average worker earns $33,140. Home providers, the fastest-growing segment at +4.3%, have no back office.
solution: Providers send attendance photos or export from Brightwheel, Procare or Kangarootime. The service validates against each program's rules, fixes errors, submits claims and chases denials. It then offers advances against verified claims, funded by a partner lender. A running library of each state's rejection codes drives the automation.
why_now: Subsidy-fraud scrutiny and attendance-verification demands rose sharply in winter 2025-26 (from memory, not verified in the brief). Universal or free-care programs are launching and the DCFSA and 45F expansions add spending. Payment-rule changes reward providers who can document cleanly.
revenue_model: 3-5% of collected subsidy revenue plus a 1.5-3% factoring fee on advances. Payroll-timing savings make it an easy sell.
non_obvious_insight: Healthcare RCM became a giant industry because the payer changed. Childcare is going through the same payer shift with no RCM industry yet. The moat is knowing each state's rejection codes and quirks, which a services-plus-software firm accumulates claim by claim.
first_30_days: Pick one state with slow, public-rule subsidy payments. Recruit 10 home providers via Facebook provider groups and the local CCR&R. Do the claims by hand with one ops hire and a spreadsheet at 4%. Log every rejection reason. Add advances through a small-business lender partner in month 2.

title: Unlisted: The Agent-Proof Offline Guide
one_liner: A numbered, mailed-only paper guide plus a human phone line for restaurants, bars, and shops that deliberately cannot be found or booked by AI agents.
customer: Affluent urbanites (30-60) paying $250-400/year, capped at about 2,000 members per city. Corporate concierge and client-gifting accounts pay $5-20k/year. Venues pay nothing, which keeps the guide's independence.
problem: ChatGPT began booking tables through OpenTable, Resy, and Yelp on 10 August 2026, and Gemini, Alexa+, and Perplexity have similar integrations. Everyone's agent now picks the same top-ranked places, bots snipe scarce tables, and Resy prohibits unsanctioned agents. 'I found this place' no longer signals taste, and small venues that want regulars rather than scale have no way to opt out of the flood.
solution: A quarterly printed booklet of 40-60 venues per city, compiled by scouts who visit anonymously. It is posted to members and never published as a PDF. Each entry has a phone number for the Unlisted line, a human-staffed concierge that books by voice, or a door code word, and never an online booking link. Fictional 'canary' details in entries let the guide trace leaks. Members agree to a no-posting norm and are expelled for breaking it. Venues get vetted, lower-no-show clientele.
why_now: Agentic booking went mainstream in August 2026 and venues are reacting with bot bans. Platform algorithms now homogenize discovery. Freelance food and travel writers are being laid off, so scout supply is cheap and high quality.
revenue_model: $250-400/year membership. Corporate concierge accounts. Paid members-only events in venues (ticketed, with the venue's cut waived). Possible city-by-city licensing to local scouts later.
non_obvious_insight: When discovery is automated, unindexability becomes the scarce good. The guide earns trust by refusing to be online, and its scarcity is enforced by physical media and an honor code. Its value is negative space that AI agents structurally cannot see.
first_30_days: Pick one city and hire 3-4 laid-off food writers as scouts. Post a teaser page with no venue names and pre-sell 300 founding memberships at $200. Print 500 numbered copies. Run the phone line on a shared business number with two part-timers. Test the model by having a scout call in a booking.

title: Exchange for Unused Grid Interconnection Headroom
one_liner: A market where owners of unused interconnection capacity and stalled queue positions sell time-sliced access to batteries and data centers that cannot wait for the queue.
customer: Sellers: owners of operating solar and wind plants whose interconnection is sized for peaks they hit only some hours a year, holders of stalled or zombie queue positions, and retiring plants holding transferable capacity rights. Buyers: battery developers, data-center developers and large electrifying industrials that need MW-scale grid access in under 24 months.
problem: Queues hold thousands of GW while data centers and storage developers wait years. Existing owners have real headroom and completed studies but no idea what they are worth or how to transfer them under FERC rules, so deals happen only through informal broker phone calls.
solution: Standardized listings: point of interconnection, headroom by hour profile (from public settlement and EIA data), completed studies and network-upgrade dollars already paid, and rule pathway (surplus interconnection service, co-location, capacity-right transfers). The platform screens deals, supports escrowed contracts and builds price discovery in $/kW-year. Later it offers time-sliced flexible contracts, for example a battery using a solar plant's line at night.
why_now: AI-driven load growth is hitting interconnection scarcity in 2026. FERC has pushed surplus and flexible interconnection, ISOs allow some capacity-right transfers, and hourly injection data makes headroom measurable for the first time.
revenue_model: 2% to 4% success fee on contract value, seller SaaS for asset managers ($1k to $3k a month for headroom analytics), and buyer-side search retainers.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable asset is not the megawatt slot; it is the completed study and network upgrades already paid for by an earlier owner, which cut years off the timeline. Most owners do not know their headroom is worth anything.
first_30_days: Use EIA and ISO settlement data plus queue files to find 150 solar plants with low peak utilization. Cold-contact 40 asset managers, sign one exclusive listing, and take a term-sheet conversation to 15 storage and data-center developers. Target one small (about 20 MW) deal for the first success fee.

title: Ticketmaster Exit Kits for Independent Venues
one_liner: A contract-audit and migration service that tells venue owners exactly when and at what cost they can leave exclusive ticketing deals, then moves them safely.
customer: Independent venue owners and operators of 500-3,000 capacity rooms in the US, and promoters who run pre-sales through those venues.
problem: A jury found Live Nation liable for illegal monopolization on 2026-04-15, and remedies remain unclear (a separate DOJ settlement dates from 2026-03-09). Venues with exclusive contracts do not know what leaving costs (liquidated damages, advance repayment, loss of fan data), and fear a botched on-sale day more than the contract.
solution: A contract analyzer that reads exclusivity, term, advance-repayment and change-of-law clauses and returns an exit date and cost sheet. Add a migration playbook (fan data export with consent, fee structure compliant with the FTC all-in rule, verified-fan pre-sales), white-label integrations with 2-3 alternative ticketing platforms, and pooled negotiation for groups of venues.
why_now: The April 2026 verdict, the FTC's all-in pricing rule (effective 2025-05-12), the state suits, and Ticketmaster's June 2026 placement inside Spotify all raise the stakes of lock-in. Venues suddenly have leverage but no capability.
revenue_model: $2-5k audit, $5-15k migration, and 10-20% of alternative platforms' fee share on the venue's tickets for three years.
non_obvious_insight: Antitrust wins create optionality, not capability. The bottleneck after a verdict is the GM's fear of a broken on-sale, so the product to sell is reduced fear, plus data ownership the venue never knew it lacked.
first_30_days: Mine the public trial exhibits for venue-contract terms and publish an exit map. Reach 10 venue GMs through independent-venue trade groups. Run three paid contract audits at $1.5k and line up two alternative ticketing partners.
